transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-09
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Tom Rivera (Halcyon ML Eng), Priya Desai (Halcyon Platform), Carlos Mendez (Halcyon CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
Quick weekly POC sync covering current prefix/KV hit rates, a new compaction-based prefetch experiment, tradeoffs on eviction tiers, and prompt canonicalization strategy. Action items: run 24h synthetic traffic with compaction, share results, price Dedicated pilot.

Topics:
- Current KV & prefix hit rate trends
- Compaction prefetch experiment (why, how)
- Prompt reuse / canonicalization approach
- Eviction policy tuning and latency regressions
- Security / VPC and enterprise checklist
- Next steps and ownership

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Alright everyone, good afternoon. Thanks for joining our weekly sync on the prefetch pilot, I think we have a short agenda—Jordan will walk through the hitrate dashboards and the new compaction run results.
[00:20] Jordan (SE): Hey all, yeah I'll jump in, quick caveat first: these numbers are from a synthetic run that mirrors reported traffic spikes, not production traffic yet so treat as directional. The key change we toggled this week was prefix compaction plus aggressive prefix coalescing before interacting with the KV store.
[00:42] Tom (Halcyon): Sorry can you repeat "compaction"? Do you mean token compaction or prompt compaction?
[00:47] Jordan (SE): Good call — prompt compaction, basically canonicalizing semantically-identical prefixes into a single key so the KV cache sees fewer unique keys. It's noisy in the transcript as kay-vee vs cv, but it's the KV.
[01:10] Priya (Halcyon): How do you decide canonicalization rules? We're worried about collapsing prompts that have user-specific tokens like appointment ids.
[01:18] Jordan (SE): Two-tier approach: first a light canonicalization (strip session IDs, timestamps) and then an optional semantic hash stage for highly repetitive templates. We keep toggles per route so you can opt out.
[01:32] Carlos (CTO): Are we losing quality when we canonicalize? Our clinical disclaimers can't be wrong.
[01:38] Jordan (SE): We measured generation delta on 200 labeled evaluation prompts. With light canonicalization the n-gram overlap drop is negligible and our quality regressions were within the acceptable threshold the team set (we log any changes to the eval harness). We also provide an escape hatch: disable canonicalization for routes flagged by you.
[02:05] Maya (AE): Jordan, show the hitrate graphs please — the one with prefix vs per-token hit.
[02:12] Jordan (SE): Pulling up slide: so baseline (no compaction) showed prefix hit ~12% across our synthetic mix, with compaction on we saw prefix hit jump to ~37% in the best bucket. KV hit was similar but more variable because the KV cache uses full prompt fingerprints. Note — the compaction run used a 48MB KV window and a two-tier TTL.
[02:40] Tom: 37% is promising, what's the latency impact at p95?
[02:44] Jordan: Median latency improved by ~8% due to fewer cold-start work, p95 was flat to +3% in worst case because compaction introduces a small extra CPU step in preprocess but reduces model tokens generated. Worth noting that we saw a small spike in tail latency when eviction pressure hit the KV store — that's from larger coalesced keys evicting more frequently if we don't adjust eviction weights.
[03:15] Priya: Eviction weights meaning?
[03:18] Jordan: We have an eviction-thermostat that balances recency vs size vs reuse-score. With compaction some keys are bigger (they represent more merged prompts) so we need to tune size penalty. We tested eviction-tier alpha values of 0.2 vs 0.5 and alpha=0.35 looked like the best tradeoff.
[03:40] Maya: Reminder — Halcyon is running in our hosted sandbox, correct? You're not on Dedicated yet?
[03:44] Tom: Correct, hosted sandbox. We want to decide if Dedicated is needed for production because of throughput predictability and some data residency asks.
[03:52] Carlos: Also SOC2 and audit logs — we need to see full KMS integration details.
[03:57] Maya: We'll send our SOC2 package plus KMS runbook; Priya if you can share who to CC for security that helps.
[04:05] Priya: Will do.
[04:12] Jordan: Back to the technicals — we also tried hybrid prefetch: we prefetch candidate KV entries only for routes with high reuse-score, and leave others to on-demand. That reduced unnecessary evictions. The hybrid approach improved economy by roughly 18% token-cost reduction in the synthetic run. The tradeoff is complexity in routing and instrumentation.
[04:45] Tom: Can you explain reuse-score?
[04:48] Jordan: It's a lightweight score computed from historical co-occurrence of prefix signatures — basically how often a head-of-conversation repeats. We compute it via rolling windows. It's noisy early but stabilizes after ~12h of traffic.
[05:05] Priya: For us it's important to preserve HIPAA controls — any prefetching or caching should avoid storing PHI. How is that addressed?
[05:13] Jordan: We have a redaction step in the preprocess pipeline; compaction runs after redaction so keys shouldn't include raw PHI. We'll add explicit test cases for PHI leakage and include the results in the next artifact.
[05:30] Carlos: Good. Cost question — if compaction increases hitrate but increases compute in preprocess, how does unit cost change?
[05:37] Jordan: For our synthetic mix the overall per-response token cost dropped ~9% after accounting for the extra CPU work. The delta depends on the split between short conversational queries and long-form generation. We'll share a cost sensitivity CSV.
[05:52] Maya: Any thoughts about session affinity? I know some pilots saw better reuse when session affinity pinning was enabled on the serving side.
[05:58] Jordan: Yes, session affinity plus prefix coalescing is complimentary. Affinity increases local KV warmness because repeated users hit the same serving shard. But affinity has tradeoffs for scale and failover. For Halcyon, given predictable user patterns, affinity might be worth testing in Dedicated mode.
[06:20] Tom: On the canonicalization rules — Priya asked about IDs; we can provide a regex list of safe tokens to drop. We'll work with Jordan on that.
[06:28] Priya: Quick Q — are you storing full prompts in logs? We prefer redacted logs only.
[06:33] Maya: We can configure logging to redact and store only fingerprints if you want. We'll include that in the security doc.
[06:40] Jordan: Small note on instrumentation — memory snapshots show the KV working set is dominated by ~8% of keys representing 60% of hits. The compaction helps by merging similar keys into that high-value set.
[06:58] Carlos: Does the compaction approach depend on model family? We use a LLaMA-variant open model; will behavior differ on other families?
[07:06] Jordan: The approach is model-agnostic at the prefix level — compaction reduces prompt space before tokenization. However model response variance interacts with hitrate because some models produce divergent completions for similar prefixes. We validated on two model families and saw similar directionality, but absolute numbers varied.
[07:30] Tom: Anything on quantization or tokenization mismatch? We had earlier issues where whitespace tokenization differences caused missed hits.
[07:36] Jordan: Good flag — compaction includes a canonical whitespace normalization step to reduce false negatives from tokenization. It's in the preprocess and should mitigate that class of misses.
[07:50] Maya: Alright, let's go to the experiment plan: Jordan, what's the 24h run config you propose?
[07:56] Jordan: Config: 24h synthetic mixed traffic (approx 200 req/sec peak), compaction on, hybrid prefetch for routes with reuse-score>0.6, eviction alpha=0.35, KV window 48MB, prefetch TTL 60s. We'll export hourly hitrate, p50/p95 latency, model token consumption, and eviction churn.
[08:18] Tom: If possible also include per-route breakdown — some clinical routes are high value.
[08:22] Jordan: Yes per-route data included.
[08:25] Priya: For Dedicated pricing — what's the minimum commit?
[08:28] Maya: I'll send the current proposal but typical pilots start with 3-month reserved capacity at a lower rate and a burst window. I'll include optional burst coverage pricing.
[08:36] Carlos: Good. Any blockers from Redwood side to run the 24h?
[08:40] Jordan: We need the representative prompt corpus from Tom to make the synthetic traffic realistic and Priya to confirm safe redaction rules. Once we have those we can kick off.
[08:50] Tom: We'll carve out the prompt corpus and share an S3 link.
[08:54] Maya: Great. Any final questions?
[09:00] Tom: On the security docs, will you provide an HSM/KMS integration plan?
[09:05] Maya: Yes, that's in the SOC2 package — I'll ask our security team to produce the HSM integration note as well.
[09:12] Carlos: Sounds good, thanks everyone.

Recap (auto):
- Compaction + prefix coalescing gave a large lift in prefix hitrate (12% -> 37% synthetically).
- Tail latency impact minimal; eviction tuning required (alpha~0.35 suggested).
- Hybrid prefetch reduces unnecessary evictions and cost; reuse-score thresholding helps.
- Security: redaction before compaction; Redwood to send SOC2 + KMS docs.
- Next: Jordan runs 24h synthetic run with proposed config; Maya sends pricing; Halcyon provides prompt corpus.

End of transcript.
